title: Why Curie's Notebooks Stay Locked
topic: Why Marie Curie's notebooks are still kept in lead-lined boxes

lines: An archivist lifts a dusty notebook, winces as a faint glow flickers.
Her colleagues laugh, saying the old papers are just ink stains.
She places the notebook on a metal tray.
A soft hiss escapes, invisible particles slipping out.
She slides the tray into a lead‑lined box.
The lid clangs, sealing the hiss inside.
You see, it’s like holding a candle in rain—without protection flame dies.
Curie's 1890s papers still contain radium‑226, whose half‑life is about 1,600 years.
That makes the notebooks radioactive for well over a thousand years.
Lead blocks the penetrating radiation, keeping the lab safe.
Anyone who wants to read them must wear protective clothing.
Ironically, the notebooks that birthed radioactivity are now the most guarded artifacts.
Even her cookbooks glow with the same deadly ink.
Researchers don gloves, goggles, and thick lead aprons before opening a box.
The air in the vault is monitored for stray particles.

claims.claim: Her papers from the 1890s are considered too dangerous to handle because of their radioactivity.
Radium‑226 has a half‑life of about 1,600 years, so her notebooks remain radioactive for well over a thousand years.
The papers are kept in lead‑lined boxes and require protective clothing to consult.
